name: style-academic
title: Formal scholarly register
description: A writing-style profile for formal scholarly prose: the register of a journal article, a thesis chapter or a conference paper. It is deliberately opposed to the conversational profiles on several metrics at once - it puts a floor under the passive voice, under hedged claims and under abstract nouns, and a ceiling over contractions and second-person address - so it is a working test of whether a band-based profile can describe two registers that contradict each other. Guidance is drawn from the ICMJE Recommendations for the Conduct, Reporting, Editing, and Publication of Scholarly Work in Medical Journals (attribution and qualified claims), APA Style Publication Manual section 4.13 (active and passive voice, at https://apastyle.apa.org/style-grammar-guidelines/grammar/active-passive-voice) and the Chicago Manual of Style Q&A on contractions in formal and technical writing (https://www.chicagomanualofstyle.org/qanda/data/faq/topics/Punctuation/faq0131.html). No guide consulted here states a rate, so every number comes from the reference corpus described below; each rule says in its own note which part of it rests on published guidance and which part rests on the corpus. The thresholds are the first thing to change. Every rule here runs on the engine's default prose gate - at least 250 words, at least 5 sentence endings, and a mean sentence between 4 and 60 words - rather than on the widened gate the other style profiles in this directory carry; corpus.note records what the widened gate admitted and why it was withdrawn.

corpus.note: Fourteen research documents in the target register - nine peer-reviewed or preprint papers from robotics, vision and applied science venues, one journal review, one working paper and one MSc thesis - extracted from PDF, with front matter, reference lists, figure captions, tables and equations removed so that only body prose is measured. One caveat governs how the numbers should be read. The selector admitted one document that is not in the target register: Learning from Demonstration for Tabletop Lab Automation is a survey written in an instructional manner ("How to Teach the Robot", "you'll", "don't"). It carries 9.8 second-person pronouns and 4.8 contractions per 1000 words where the other thirteen carry 0.0 and at most 0.4, and it also supplies the corpus maximum on hedging. It is left in the corpus because removing a document after seeing its numbers is how a distribution gets fitted to a conclusion, but every rule now reports two reference figures - one over all fourteen documents and one over the thirteen that are in register - and the second is the one the edges rest on. Quantiles are linear-interpolated between the two central observations; min and max are the observed extremes. Edges are stated per rule and are mostly set outside the observed range rather than at p10 and p90, because thirteen documents is a thin basis for a two-sided interval. The false-positive corpus is 16 documents / 19,555 words of human-written engineering documentation under /home/bas/Downloads: every document of 250 words or more that clears the engine's default prose gate. An earlier draft widened that gate to maxSentenceWords 200 and minSentenceWords 1 and measured 18 documents instead. The two extra documents were a Python source file pasted into a .txt and a README that is headings, bullets and code blocks, at 79.5 and 135.8 words per apparent sentence; between them they produced 13 of the profile's 87 findings, including a report that a Python module carries too few abstract nouns. The gate is back at the engine default and the profile now reports 74 findings in 16 files. Two kinds of noise survive that gate and are worth knowing about. Markdown and HTML tables are extracted as running text, so their cells count as words and the thousands separator in a figure like 11,045 counts as a comma; running this profile with --skip-tables takes the local count from 74 findings to 68 and is the right setting for documentation. And a file that mixes prose with console output, tracebacks or version strings is measured as one document, because a file extension followed by a space reads as the end of a sentence: three of the four local documents that report on sentence-length variation are of that kind rather than prose that lurches. Two further limits: superscript numeral citations do not survive PDF text extraction, so the citation rate is measured low, and the corpus is entirely technical, so a profile fitted to it will read history or philosophy as off target. These are the first numbers to retune.

voice: Third person about the subject, first person about the work. Claims carry their scope inside the sentence. Where the actor adds nothing, the measurement goes to the front of the clause. Verbs written out in full. Every claim that is not the document’s own is attached to a source, and every claim the evidence only partly reaches is marked as such.

tension.note: candidates/economist.json reports a pile-up at or above 70 nominalisations per 1000 words. The median of this profile's reference corpus is 76.1 over the thirteen documents that are in register, and running that rule over the corpus reports it in 10 of the 14 files, so an ordinary research paper reports there. Both readings are correct: the prose really is describing rather than doing, and that really is what this register asks for. Those findings stand. If you disagree with that rule for your own writing, put nominalisation-pileup in the ignore list of your own slop.json.

rules/simonwillison.json reports consecutive sentences that share a literal four-word skeleton. This is the largest interaction between this profile and the shipped detector, and it is measured: echo-triad reports 115 times across all 14 reference documents, 1.19 per 1000 words, against 0.30 per 1000 in the local engineering corpus. The cause is a convention rather than an accident. A methods section defines things in parallel - "The x-axis is defined by the centres of Spheres 1 and 2. The xy-plane is defined by the centres of the three spheres." - and technical prose repeats a term instead of varying it, because renaming the same quantity twice is how a reader loses track of it. Both readings are correct: those really are parallel sentences, and parallelism really is how this register states a definition. The findings stand, and nothing in this profile relaxes that rule.

candidates/slop-gate.json reports a list of single words, five of which are ordinary in this register: moreover, robust, leverage, crucial and in-conclusion. Over the reference corpus that set reports 170 times across all 14 documents, 1.75 per 1000 words - moreover 71, robust 62, leverage 18, crucial 9, in-conclusion 5 - against 3 findings and 0.10 per 1000 in the local engineering corpus, a seventeen-fold difference between the registers. Two of those words are the register's plain vocabulary rather than its ornament: "moreover" is a connective, and "robust" names a specific property in control, statistics and estimation for which there is no shorter synonym. This profile makes no claim about individual words and does not relax that set. The findings stand, and a technical term you intend to keep belongs in the ignore list of your own slop.json.

candidates/humanizer-de.json reports sentence-length variation at or below 0.40. The reference corpus for this profile ran 0.48 to 0.86, and running that rule over the corpus reports it in 0 of the 14 documents, so this is a gap rather than a live disagreement: nothing in the register as measured actually lands there. An earlier version of this note said a paper a little flatter than the median lands in that rule's territory, and the measurement does not support it - the median is 0.61 and the edge is 0.40. What is true is that eight hundredths of a coefficient separate that edge from the flattest paper measured here, so a paper slightly flatter than any in this corpus would land there while still sitting inside this register. At cv 0.38 the prose is both genuinely metrically even and genuinely in register. That finding stands.

rules/wikipedia-ai.json reports the "it is important to note that" family of formulae wherever they appear, and its participle-tail rule reports the ", demonstrating that ..." clause that closes a scholarly paragraph. Both are long-standing scholarly formulae and this register uses them without embarrassment. Over the reference corpus that set reports note-that 11 times and participle-tail 8 times across the 14 documents, against 0 of each in 30,300 words of local engineering prose, so these are register signals rather than accidents. The findings stand; this profile has no opinion on individual wordings, only on rates.

rules.name: Fewer attributed sources than this register carries
rules.description: Attributed sources per 1000 words: bracketed numerals and author-date parentheticals. Below the floor the document is asserting more than it attributes.
rules.suggest: Below the academic floor (2 attributed sources per 1000 words). Attach the claims that are not your own to a named source.
rules.note: A measurement of fit, not a defect: a methods section, a proof or a piece of primary reporting legitimately sits below this floor. This is the metric that separates a qualified claim from an unattributed one, and it composes with wikipedia-ai/vague-experts rather than competing with it: that rule reports “experts argue” and “studies suggest” wherever they appear, and this one reports a document that qualifies its claims without naming anyone at all. A document that reads high on hedging and low here is the case both measurements are pointing at. The two reference documents below the floor are both explainable: one is the out-of-register survey named in corpus.note, and one is a journal article whose superscript numerals did not survive text extraction from the PDF, so the true reference floor is higher than the number above. Read the local rate of 15 in 16 with that in mind - a corpus of engineering READMEs and troubleshooting notes cites nothing at all, and this edge separates registers far more sharply than it separates documents inside one. It still discriminates within the corpus: the two technical-position papers are outside only 2 of the 11 edges in this profile, the chattiest guide is outside 6, and no document is outside all 11. Shipped one-sided, and by measurement rather than oversight: a ceiling would have to sit above the reference maximum of 13.0, where neither corpus holds a single document, so it would report nothing. A review that cites on every line is still in this register. Selecting this profile is the statement that you want this register, so the fix is an instruction, not a question. If the band is wrong for this document, move it with `tune` in slop.json or drop the profile; do not leave the finding unaddressed on the grounds that the register is a choice.
rules.measured: floor 2 /1000. Reference corpus, 14 documents / 116,073 words: 0.0 (min) / 6.3 (median) / 13.0 (max), with 2 at or below the floor; over the 13 documents that are in register: 0.0 / 6.5 / 13.0, with 1 at or below it. Local corpus, 16 documents / 19,555 words of engineering prose that clear the prose gate: 0.0 / 0.0 / 3.5, with 15 of 16 below it. The floor sits between the reference p10 of 0.7 and p25 of 3.3.

hit: Here's the thing about calibration that nobody tells you when you start. You'll spend a week fighting the camera mount and then you'll find out the real problem was the cable. I've done this on four robots now and it goes the same way every time. You think it's a maths problem. It isn't. It's a hardware problem wearing a maths costume. The first robot I built had a lovely calibration routine and a bracket made of laser-cut acrylic. Guess which one moved. If your bracket flexes by half a millimetre when the arm swings you can throw away everything the solver told you. So buy the aluminium one. It costs forty dollars and it saves you a fortnight. Here's what I do now before I touch any code at all. I grab the camera and I wiggle it. If I can feel any play in it I stop right there and go find a machinist. Then I run the arm through its full range and I watch the mount like a hawk. You can see flex if you look for it. Only then do I open the laptop. The second thing nobody tells you is that your data collection matters far more than your solver. I used to think the clever solver was the interesting part. It really isn't. Grab twice as many poses from twice as many angles and the boring solver will beat the clever one every time. Take the extra twenty minutes. Your future self will thank you when the numbers stop drifting. And when it does go wrong, and it will, start at the bracket and work inwards. That order has never let me down. It's dull advice. It's also the advice I wish somebody had given me on my first day with a robot arm and a webcam. You'll ignore it anyway. Everybody does. Then you'll buy the aluminium bracket.

The rig holds the camera. A bracket carries the load. The bracket bolts to the frame. Four bolts hold it. Each bolt takes a washer. The frame sits on rubber feet. The feet damp vibration. The compressor next door is loud. Without the feet the images blur. We learned that fast. The camera looks down. It sees a printed target. The target is a checkerboard. It sits on glass. Glass keeps the pattern flat. Paper does not stay flat. A warped target biases every pose. The bias is small at first. It grows with distance. The arm moves the target. It runs a fixed sequence. The sequence covers the volume. It takes eleven minutes. An operator watches the first pass. Then she walks away. The software records each image. It records the joint angles too. Both streams share a clock. One clock is enough. Two clocks need a sync model. The solver reads both streams. It returns a transform. It prints a residual. Under one millimetre passes. Anything else fails. Failures go back to the bracket. We check the bolts. Then we check the feet. Then we check the target. The solver is never the problem. It is the mount. Or the target. Or the clock. The runbook says so. New operators ignore that line. They come back later. Then they read it again. Then they check the bolts. The rig has run for four years. It has never surprised us. That is the whole point of it. Boring hardware makes boring data. Boring data makes good numbers. Good numbers make short meetings. Nobody writes papers about brackets. Somebody probably should. The bracket is the experiment. The solver is arithmetic. We keep forgetting that. Then the mount moves again.
miss: The relationship between extrinsic calibration and estimation accuracy has drawn steady attention since factor-graph formulations reached inertial navigation (Kaess et al., 2012). Early treatments assumed that the rigid transform between camera and inertial unit had been fixed in advance by a separate procedure, an assumption that proved untenable in the field, where thermal cycling and mechanical shock move the sensors relative to one another [7]. Later work relaxed the assumption by carrying the transform in the estimated state, at the cost of a larger optimisation problem and a longer collection session. The tension between observability and tractability is usually resolved in favour of tractability, though the grounds for that preference are rarely stated in the published descriptions. Our evaluation suggests that the resulting loss of orientation accuracy is smaller than earlier accounts of the problem indicate, provided the mounting assembly is stiff and the thermal environment stays inside the range over which the calibration ran (Furgale, 2013). We gathered the measurements reported here over eleven sessions, under lighting that ranged from overcast daylight to sodium street lamps, and two independent observers labelled each session. A third reader with access to the raw inertial traces settled their disagreements. The distribution of orientation error appears roughly symmetric, which is consistent with the zero-mean noise the derivation assumes. We saw a residual correlation with temperature in three of the eleven sessions, and its magnitude was around four per cent of the total variance [12]. That correlation is likely attributable to expansion of the mounting bracket rather than to any property of the estimator. The competing account, a slow drift in the inertial bias, is hard to rule out on the present evidence, and a dedicated thermal study of the assembly would be needed to separate the two. For practitioners the implication is narrow. The calibration holds across the operating range examined here, so long as the thermal envelope is respected. Beyond that envelope nobody has examined the assumptions behind the derivation, and extending these conclusions to warmer installations is not warranted by what we measured. Comparable limits appear in evaluations of related estimation frameworks (Rehder and Siegwart, 2017). The contribution of this section is therefore a measurement of a known limitation rather than its removal.

rules.name: Fewer qualified claims than this register makes
rules.description: Epistemic qualifiers per 1000 words: may, might, suggests, indicates, appears, likely, approximately and their neighbours. Below the floor the conclusions are stated flat, without marking how far the evidence reaches.
rules.suggest: Below the academic floor (1.5 qualifiers per 1000 words). Mark the claims the evidence only partly reaches.
rules.note: A measurement of fit, not a defect: a specification, a runbook or a set of instructions is written flat on purpose. Sourced from the ICMJE Recommendations, whose guidance for the discussion section is to “link the conclusions with the goals of the study” while keeping clear of “unqualified statements and conclusions not adequately supported by the data”, and which adds “state new hypotheses when warranted, but label them clearly”. Several sets in this project report hedging constructions as phrases - structural/hedge-then-affirm and wikipedia-ai/vague-experts are the two - and those are one-sided reports on particular wordings, while this is a floor on the rate. Neither of them reports anywhere in the reference corpus, so following this floor does not walk a document into either. Shipped one-sided after measurement, not by default: over-qualification is a real way to leave this register, but the only document in either corpus above 8.1 per 1000 is the out-of-register survey at 13.1, and a ceiling fitted to it would be fitted to a document that is not in the register at all. The local maximum is 5.3, so a ceiling would report nothing there either. This is the metric that most deserves a second edge once a wider reference corpus can put one on firm ground. Selecting this profile is the statement that you want this register, so the fix is an instruction, not a question. If the band is wrong for this document, move it with `tune` in slop.json or drop the profile; do not leave the finding unaddressed on the grounds that the register is a choice.
rules.measured: floor 1.5 /1000. Reference corpus, 14 documents / 116,073 words: 0.9 (min) / 4.6 (median) / 13.1 (max), with 1 at or below the floor; over the 13 in-register documents: 0.9 / 4.5 / 8.1, with 1 at or below it. The corpus maximum of 13.1 belongs to the out-of-register survey named in corpus.note, so the highest rate any paper in the register carries is 8.1. Local corpus, 16 documents / 19,555 words: 0.0 / 1.0 / 5.3, with 10 of 16 below it. The floor sits just under the reference p10 of 1.7.

rules.name: Passive constructions outside the rate this register uses
rules.description: Passive constructions per 1000 words, counted as a form of “be” followed by a participle. Below the band nearly every clause puts an actor in front; above it almost none does, and the reader has to reconstruct who did what.
rules.suggest: Outside the academic band (4.5 to 30 passives per 1000 words). Below it, put the measurement or the sample at the front of the clause where the person who handled it adds nothing. Above it, name the actor in the passages where the actor is the point.
rules.note: A measurement of fit, not a defect: most registers put the actor in front, which is why the low rate reads as a virtue elsewhere, and two of the fourteen reference papers sit above the high edge and both are readable. The count is a proxy rather than a parse. It misses participles held away from the auxiliary by an adverb, and irregular participles ending in neither -ed nor -en; every number quoted carries the same undercount, so the edges and the measurement agree with one another. This is the clearest inversion in the profile. APA Style, Publication Manual section 4.13, recommends the active voice “as much as possible” and then states that the passive is “acceptable in expository writing” and where the focus falls on the object or recipient of the action rather than on the actor - which describes most of a methods section. A conversational profile puts a ceiling on the same metric; this one puts a floor under it, and both are correct about their own register. This edge is the lower half of a genuine two-sided band: style-academic-passive-high carries the upper half, and a document between 4.5 and 30 per 1000 hears nothing from either. Selecting this profile is the statement that you want this register, so the fix is an instruction, not a question. If the band is wrong for this document, move it with `tune` in slop.json or drop the profile; do not leave the finding unaddressed on the grounds that the register is a choice.
rules.measured: band 4.5-30 /1000. Reference corpus, 14 documents / 116,073 words: 4.2 (min) / 11.1 (median) / 30.9 (max), with 1 at or below this edge; over the 13 in-register documents: 4.2 / 11.4 / 30.9, with 1 at or below it. Local corpus, 16 documents / 19,555 words: 0.0 / 2.3 / 8.5, with 12 of 16 below it. The floor is the reference p7. A floor of 4.0 was measured first and rejected: it clears the reference minimum of 4.16 by only four per cent.  Upper edge: band 4.5-30 /1000. The reference p90 is 28.1 and the maximum 30.9, so this edge is the reference p86 and 2 of the 14 documents sit on or above it - a conference paper at 30.9 and an MSc thesis at 30.8, both of them in register. No document in the 16-document local corpus reaches it, its maximum being 8.5. A ceiling of 35 was measured first and rejected because it reports in neither corpus, which is a rule measuring nothing.

The mounting assembly was designed by the mechanical team and reviewed by two engineers before the drawings went out. The bracket was machined from a single aluminium billet, and the mating faces were ground flat after the initial cut. Dowel pins were pressed into the plate so the camera can come off and go back on without a fresh calibration. The completed assembly then went to the integration bench, where it was fitted to the arm and the loom was routed along the inner face of the second link. That routing was chosen so the cable would not stretch at the extremes of travel. Once the hardware came together the calibration sequence ran three times and the residuals were logged in the shared record. Images were captured at a fixed exposure, and frames in which the target was partly occluded were discarded before the solver ran. Joint angles were read from the controller at the instant each shutter released, and both streams were stamped with one clock, so no synchronisation model was needed. The resulting transform was compared against the value obtained on the previous rig, and the difference fell well inside the tolerance in the specification. A thermal soak then ran for nine hours, during which the ambient temperature climbed from four degrees to thirty-eight degrees in eight steps. At each step the sequence repeated and the residual went into the log. No drift was detected beyond the noise floor of the measurement. The assembly was therefore accepted, the drawings were archived, and the procedure was written into the runbook so the next rig can be built without the questions that held this one up. Three further assemblies have since been produced to the same drawing and none of them has been rejected at the bench.

rules.name: More contractions than this register uses
rules.description: Contractions per 1000 words: n’t forms, and it’s, you’re, we’ve, I’ll. Possessive apostrophes are not counted. Above the ceiling the sentences are taking the spoken form of the verb.
rules.suggest: Above the academic ceiling (3 contractions per 1000 words). Write the verb out in full.
rules.note: A measurement of fit, not a defect: in every other register the contracted form is the natural one. hit: Here's the thing about calibration that nobody tells you when you start. You'll spend a week fighting the camera mount and then you'll find out the real problem was the cable. I've done this on four robots now and it goes the same way every time. You think it's a maths problem. It isn't. It's a hardware problem wearing a maths costume. The first robot I built had a lovely calibration routine and a bracket made of laser-cut acrylic. Guess which one moved. If your bracket flexes by half a millimetre when the arm swings you can throw away everything the solver told you. So buy the aluminium one. It costs forty dollars and it saves you a fortnight. Here's what I do now before I touch any code at all. I grab the camera and I wiggle it. If I can feel any play in it I stop right there and go find a machinist. Then I run the arm through its full range and I watch the mount like a hawk. You can see flex if you look for it. Only then do I open the laptop. The second thing nobody tells you is that your data collection matters far more than your solver. I used to think the clever solver was the interesting part. It really isn't. Grab twice as many poses from twice as many angles and the boring solver will beat the clever one every time. Take the extra twenty minutes. Your future self will thank you when the numbers stop drifting. And when it does go wrong, and it will, start at the bracket and work inwards. That order has never let me down. It's dull advice. It's also the advice I wish somebody had given me on my first day with a robot arm and a webcam. You'll ignore it anyway. Everybody does. Then you'll buy the aluminium bracket.
miss: The relationship between extrinsic calibration and estimation accuracy has drawn steady attention since factor-graph formulations reached inertial navigation (Kaess et al., 2012). Early treatments assumed that the rigid transform between camera and inertial unit had been fixed in advance by a separate procedure, an assumption that proved untenable in the field, where thermal cycling and mechanical shock move the sensors relative to one another [7]. Later work relaxed the assumption by carrying the transform in the estimated state, at the cost of a larger optimisation problem and a longer collection session. The tension between observability and tractability is usually resolved in favour of tractability, though the grounds for that preference are rarely stated in the published descriptions. Our evaluation suggests that the resulting loss of orientation accuracy is smaller than earlier accounts of the problem indicate, provided the mounting assembly is stiff and the thermal environment stays inside the range over which the calibration ran (Furgale, 2013). We gathered the measurements reported here over eleven sessions, under lighting that ranged from overcast daylight to sodium street lamps, and two independent observers labelled each session. A third reader with access to the raw inertial traces settled their disagreements. The distribution of orientation error appears roughly symmetric, which is consistent with the zero-mean noise the derivation assumes. We saw a residual correlation with temperature in three of the eleven sessions, and its magnitude was around four per cent of the total variance [12]. That correlation is likely attributable to expansion of the mounting bracket rather than to any property of the estimator. The competing account, a slow drift in the inertial bias, is hard to rule out on the present evidence, and a dedicated thermal study of the assembly would be needed to separate the two. For practitioners the implication is narrow. The calibration holds across the operating range examined here, so long as the thermal envelope is respected. Beyond that envelope nobody has examined the assumptions behind the derivation, and extending these conclusions to warmer installations is not warranted by what we measured. Comparable limits appear in evaluations of related estimation frameworks (Rehder and Siegwart, 2017). The contribution of this section is therefore a measurement of a known limitation rather than its removal.

The rig holds the camera above the workbench. A steel bracket carries the load. The bracket bolts to the frame at four points. Each bolt takes a washer and a nut. The frame itself sits on rubber feet. The feet damp the vibration from the compressor next door. Without them the images blur at the longest exposure. We learned that the hard way in the first week. The camera looks down at a printed target. The target is a checkerboard on a sheet of glass. Glass keeps the pattern flat. Paper does not. A warped target puts a bias into every pose. The bias is small at short range. It grows with distance from the optical axis. The arm moves the target through a fixed sequence of poses. The sequence covers the whole working volume. It takes eleven minutes to run. An operator watches the first pass and then walks away. The software records one image at each pose. It also records the joint angles from the controller. Both streams carry a timestamp from the same clock. That single clock matters more than anything else in the rig. Two clocks would need a sync protocol and a drift model. One clock needs neither. The solver reads both streams and returns a transform. It prints the residual in millimetres. A residual under one millimetre passes. Anything above that goes back to the bracket. We check the bolts first. Then we check the feet. Then we check the target for warp. In four years the answer has never been the solver itself. It is always the mount or the target or the clock. The runbook says so in the first line. New operators read that line and ignore it. They come back three hours later and read it again. Then they check the bolts. The rig has run for four years without a surprise.

rules.name: Sentence length outside the range this register keeps
rules.description: Sentence endings per 1000 words, which is mean sentence length upside down. Below the band the average sentence carries several clauses at once; above it each sentence carries one proposition, with the relations between them left for the reader to infer.
rules.suggest: Outside the academic band (28 to 62 sentence endings per 1000 words, an average sentence of 16 to 36 words). Below it, end one of the longest sentences early and let the qualification stand on its own. Above it, join the propositions whose relation to each other is part of the claim.
rules.note: A measurement of fit, not a defect: long periodic sentences are a legitimate scholarly manner and older journals are full of them, and short sentences are the plainest way to be understood. Two things limit what this edge can see. The measurement is sentence endings, so anything that ends a line without a full stop - a heading, a table row, a list item - lengthens the apparent sentence without lengthening any sentence a reader meets, and a document built mostly of those will read as long-winded when it is not built of sentences at all. The prose gate then draws the line: a document whose mean sentence runs over 60 words is not measured, so this edge reports long-winded prose between roughly 36 and 60 words a sentence and goes quiet above that. On the local corpus everything above the 60-word line was a source file or a bullet list rather than prose, so the gate earns its place there, but a genuinely periodic essay at 70 words a sentence would go unreported and that is a real hole. This edge is the lower half of a two-sided band; style-academic-sentence-length-short carries the upper half. hit: The relationship between extrinsic calibration and downstream estimation accuracy has received sustained attention since the introduction of factor-graph formulations for inertial navigation. The early treatments of the problem uniformly assumed that the rigid transformation between the camera and the inertial measurement unit had been determined in advance by some separate procedure whose failure modes were rarely discussed. That assumption proved untenable in field deployments, where thermal cycling and mechanical shock displace the sensors relative to one another by amounts that are small in absolute terms but entirely sufficient to dominate the orientation error budget of any estimator that treats the transformation as a fixed quantity rather than as something to be recovered alongside the trajectory. Subsequent investigations relaxed the requirement by including the transformation in the estimated state vector, at the cost of a substantial increase in the dimensionality of the optimisation problem and a corresponding increase in the number of poses required before the parameters become observable at all, which in practice means a longer and more carefully designed data collection session. The tension between observability and computational tractability is generally resolved in favour of tractability, although the justification for that preference is rarely made explicit in the published descriptions of the resulting systems. A reader attempting to reproduce the reported accuracy figures will often discover that the missing detail was precisely the one that mattered. Our own evaluation suggests that the degradation in orientation accuracy attributable to a fixed-transformation assumption is smaller than the earlier characterisations of the problem indicate, provided that the mounting assembly is stiff and the thermal environment stays within the range over which the calibration was performed, two conditions that are easy to state and surprisingly difficult to guarantee on a mobile platform. The measurements reported here were collected over eleven sessions under illumination conditions that varied from overcast daylight to sodium street lighting, and each session was annotated independently by two observers whose disagreements were resolved by a third annotator with access to the raw inertial traces rather than to the images alone. A residual correlation with ambient temperature was detected in three of those eleven sessions and its magnitude was estimated at approximately four per cent of the total variance, a figure that is small enough to be ignored in most deployments and large enough to matter in the one deployment for which the system was originally commissioned. The most plausible account of that correlation attributes it to thermal expansion of the mounting bracket rather than to any property of the estimator itself. A competing account attributing it to a slow drift in the inertial bias cannot be excluded on the evidence presently available and would require a dedicated thermal characterisation of the assembly to settle one way or the other. The practical implication for anyone reproducing this work is that the calibration retains its validity across the operating range examined here provided the thermal envelope is respected, and that extending the conclusions to warmer installations is not warranted by the measurements that were actually taken. A further consideration, and one that the literature on this problem has treated only in passing, is the degree to which the annotation procedure itself introduces a bias into the reported figures, since the observers were aware of the hypothesis under test and were working from the same images that the estimator consumed rather than from an independent record of the platform's motion. The most defensible response available to us was to require agreement between two observers before a session entered the analysis, and to route the remaining disagreements to a third reader who worked from the inertial traces alone, an arrangement that removes the most obvious route by which an expectation could propagate into the numbers without pretending that the procedure is now free of every such route. Whether a fully blinded protocol would change the reported figures materially is a question this work does not settle, and the honest summary of the position is that the effect reported here is large enough to survive a bias of the size that the annotation procedure could plausibly introduce, but not so large that the question can be set aside altogether in any replication of the work.

The rig holds the camera. A bracket carries the load. The bracket bolts to the frame. Four bolts hold it. Each bolt takes a washer. The frame sits on rubber feet. The feet damp vibration. The compressor next door is loud. Without the feet the images blur. We learned that fast. The camera looks down. It sees a printed target. The target is a checkerboard. It sits on glass. Glass keeps the pattern flat. Paper does not stay flat. A warped target biases every pose. The bias is small at first. It grows with distance. The arm moves the target. It runs a fixed sequence. The sequence covers the volume. It takes eleven minutes. An operator watches the first pass. Then she walks away. The software records each image. It records the joint angles too. Both streams share a clock. One clock is enough. Two clocks need a sync model. The solver reads both streams. It returns a transform. It prints a residual. Under one millimetre passes. Anything else fails. Failures go back to the bracket. We check the bolts. Then we check the feet. Then we check the target. The solver is never the problem. It is the mount. Or the target. Or the clock. The runbook says so. New operators ignore that line. They come back later. Then they read it again. Then they check the bolts. The rig has run for four years. It has never surprised us. That is the whole point of it. Boring hardware makes boring data. Boring data makes good numbers. Good numbers make short meetings. Nobody writes papers about brackets. Somebody probably should. The bracket is the experiment. The solver is arithmetic. We keep forgetting that. Then the mount moves again.
miss: The relationship between extrinsic calibration and estimation accuracy has drawn steady attention since factor-graph formulations reached inertial navigation (Kaess et al., 2012). Early treatments assumed that the rigid transform between camera and inertial unit had been fixed in advance by a separate procedure, an assumption that proved untenable in the field, where thermal cycling and mechanical shock move the sensors relative to one another [7]. Later work relaxed the assumption by carrying the transform in the estimated state, at the cost of a larger optimisation problem and a longer collection session. The tension between observability and tractability is usually resolved in favour of tractability, though the grounds for that preference are rarely stated in the published descriptions. Our evaluation suggests that the resulting loss of orientation accuracy is smaller than earlier accounts of the problem indicate, provided the mounting assembly is stiff and the thermal environment stays inside the range over which the calibration ran (Furgale, 2013). We gathered the measurements reported here over eleven sessions, under lighting that ranged from overcast daylight to sodium street lamps, and two independent observers labelled each session. A third reader with access to the raw inertial traces settled their disagreements. The distribution of orientation error appears roughly symmetric, which is consistent with the zero-mean noise the derivation assumes. We saw a residual correlation with temperature in three of the eleven sessions, and its magnitude was around four per cent of the total variance [12]. That correlation is likely attributable to expansion of the mounting bracket rather than to any property of the estimator. The competing account, a slow drift in the inertial bias, is hard to rule out on the present evidence, and a dedicated thermal study of the assembly would be needed to separate the two. For practitioners the implication is narrow. The calibration holds across the operating range examined here, so long as the thermal envelope is respected. Beyond that envelope nobody has examined the assumptions behind the derivation, and extending these conclusions to warmer installations is not warranted by what we measured. Comparable limits appear in evaluations of related estimation frameworks (Rehder and Siegwart, 2017). The contribution of this section is therefore a measurement of a known limitation rather than its removal.

rules.name: Sentence length swings more than this register keeps it
rules.description: Sentence-length variation, as standard deviation over mean. Above the ceiling the prose swings between very short sentences and very long ones, making its emphasis by rhythm.
rules.suggest: Above the academic ceiling (sentence-length variation 1.05). Even out the extremes so the emphasis comes from the argument rather than from the metre.
rules.note: A measurement of fit, not a defect: the swing is a deliberate effect in most other registers. Shipped one-sided on purpose. A low edge would have to sit near 0.42 to stay under the reference minimum of 0.48, and humanizer-de/uniform-sentence-length already reports at or below 0.40; two edges five per cent apart, on a statistic that markup mutation moves, is not a band anyone could rely on, and no fixture could clear both by the 20 per cent this profile asks. Worth being exact about the size of that overlap, because the tension entry used to overstate it: running humanizer-de over the reference corpus reports uniform-sentence-length in 0 of the 14 documents, so what sits between 0.40 and 0.48 is a gap rather than a live disagreement about any real paper. See the tension entry for what happens inside it. One extraction caveat belongs with the number: the coefficient is computed over splits at sentence terminators, so a version string, a file extension or a line of console output inside a document reads as a very short sentence and pushes the variation up. Of the four local documents that report here, three mix prose with terminal output, and --skip-tables removes one of them. Selecting this profile is the statement that you want this register, so the fix is an instruction, not a question. If the band is wrong for this document, move it with `tune` in slop.json or drop the profile; do not leave the finding unaddressed on the grounds that the register is a choice.
rules.measured: ceiling cv 1.05. Reference corpus, 14 documents / 116,073 words: 0.48 (min) / 0.61 (median) / 0.86 (max), so none reaches it, and the 13 in-register documents give the same range. Local corpus, 16 documents / 19,555 words: 0.49 / 0.78 / 1.53, with 4 of 16 at or above it. The edge is 22 per cent above the reference maximum.

hit: The mount failed. Over the following eleven weeks the team assembled a complete thermal characterisation of the mounting assembly, running the arm through its full range of motion at ambient temperatures from four degrees to thirty-eight degrees while logging the residual reported by the solver at every pose in the sequence, which produced a dataset large enough to settle a question that had been open since the very first deployment of the rig. Nobody was surprised. The bracket moved. It always had. What followed was a redesign that replaced the laser-cut acrylic plate with a milled aluminium one, added a second pair of dowel pins to constrain the remaining degree of freedom, and moved the whole assembly forward by nineteen millimetres so that the camera no longer sat directly above the heat sink of the onboard computer, an arrangement that in hindsight nobody on the team could defend. It worked. The residual dropped. Everyone moved on. Across the whole of the subsequent validation campaign, which ran for a further six weeks and covered the same temperature range as the characterisation that had motivated the redesign in the first place, the solver never once reported a residual above the one millimetre threshold that the runbook had specified since the very first version of the document was written. That was the end of it. The bracket was the answer. It had been the answer for three years, in every incident review, in every postmortem document, and in every conversation that began with somebody asking whether the estimator itself might be at fault, and yet the acrylic plate survived four generations of the rig because it was cheap and because replacing it required a machinist. Nobody wanted the machinist. The machinist was expensive. The bracket was not.
